lessons.title: Daily bite
lessons.objective: You can recall today's due concepts in three minutes.

payload.prompt: How does a referee make up for time lost to injuries and delays?

options.text: Adds the lost time at the end of each half
Stops the clock during every stoppage
Plays a fixed extra five minutes every time

explanation.correct: Right. The clock keeps running through the ninety minutes, and the referee adds the time lost at the end of each half.
explanation.incorrect: Football does not stop the clock. Time lost to injuries and delays is added on at the end of each half.
explanation.sayThisLine: The clock never stops, they just add the time on.

payload.prompt: At the moment the pass is played, the receiver's shoulder is level with the second-last defender. Offside?

scene.alt: A passer plays the ball forward at the moment the receiver's shoulder is level with the second-last opponent.

explanation.correct: No, he's onside. Level with the second-last defender counts as onside; the attacker gets the benefit.
explanation.incorrect: Level is onside. Only a part of the body that can score (head, body or legs) nearer the goal line than the second-last defender and the ball puts you in an offside position.
explanation.sayThisLine: Level is onside, so the goal stands.

payload.template: Expected goals (xG) rates the {{quality}} of a chance by how likely it was to become a {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Right. xG rates how good a chance was, based on things like shot position and angle, whether or not it went in.
explanation.incorrect: xG measures the probability that a shot becomes a goal, based on factors like distance and angle, independent of whether it went in.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: We lost 1-0 but won the xG 2.1 to 0.3, so we played better.

payload.question: What is he saying?

options.text: His team created better chances but didn't finish
His team lost unfairly
The xG explains why they underperformed
The opponent got lucky

payload.translation: His team created chances worth 2.1 expected goals against the opponent's 0.3; the final score doesn't reflect who played better.

followUps.line: Do you think they'll score more next time?
followUps.why: Shows you understand regression to the mean.

followUps.line: What was the big chance they missed?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: xG is a tool to talk about luck and finishing; don't use it to argue the scoreline didn't matter.

pairs.definition: The standard 90 minutes of a match (two 45-minute halves).
Minutes the referee adds at the end of each half to compensate for stoppages.
Thirty minutes (two 15-minute periods) played after a knockout match if still level after ninety.

explanation.summary: Most matches end at 90 minutes plus added time. Only knockouts that are tied go to extra time.
explanation.sayThisLine: It went to extra time and they won it in the second period.

lessons.title: Weekly rewind
lessons.objective: You can revisit last week's concepts at a slower pace.

payload.prompt: A team plays a 4-2-3-1. What does the '2' represent?

options.text: Two strikers
Two holding midfielders in front of the defence
Two wingers

explanation.correct: Right. The 4-2-3-1 has four at the back, then two deep midfielders screening, three in the middle, and one striker.
explanation.incorrect: The numbers read from defence to attack: four defenders, two holding mids (the 'six' and 'eight'), three attacking players, and one striker.
explanation.sayThisLine: In a 4-2-3-1 the twos sit in front of the back four.

payload.prompt: A midfielder passes back to his keeper and the other team presses together. That is a pressing trigger. True or false?

scene.alt: A midfielder passes backward to the goalkeeper, and the opposing team immediately presses together.

explanation.correct: True. A back pass is a classic pressing trigger; it signals danger and the team jumps.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a backwards pass is a sign of danger and a trigger for a coordinated press.
explanation.sayThisLine: Back pass, that's the trigger, they all go together.

payload.template: A corner routine is a {{type}} plan where the team decides {{what}}.

explanation.correct: Right. A corner routine is a set play: the team practises where the ball will go and who runs where.
explanation.incorrect: A corner routine is a planned set piece. The attacking team rehearses the delivery, near-post runs, and far-post targets.

payload.prompt: Match the pressing type to where it happens.

pairs.definition: Closing opponents down in their own half, winning the ball close to their goal.
Defending in the middle third, then pressing when the ball enters your zone.
Defending deep near your box, inviting possession while staying compact.

explanation.summary: These three defensive approaches describe where and how aggressively you close opponents down.
explanation.sayThisLine: They pressed high, but we played out the back and broke it.

statement.speaker: Sophie
statement.text: That near post flick was so well drilled, the far post man was waiting.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: A lucky corner goal
A planned set-piece move with two players
A rehearsed near-post flick and a waiting far-post player
Spontaneous attacking play

payload.translation: Her team has a corner routine where a player flicks the ball at the near post and a teammate times their run to tap in at the far post. It's a planned move, not luck.

followUps.line: How many corner goals does your team score?
Do they practise corner routines a lot?
followUps.why: Shows you know set pieces are coached.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Set-piece coaching is real and often hidden; it's fine to ask.

lessons.title: Say-this lightning round
lessons.objective: You can decode fan lines quickly.

statement.speaker: Marcus
statement.text: That was a worldie, top bins from thirty yards.

payload.question: What does 'worldie' mean?

options.text: A spectacular goal from distance or an unlikely angle
A goal in the World Cup
The best goal of the season
A goal that was impossible to save

payload.translation: He scored an incredible goal from thirty yards out, striking it into the top corner. A 'worldie' is a spectacular, audacious goal.

followUps.line: Do you have a favourite worldie from this season?
Was that from open play or a set piece?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't remember it, ask him to describe it; that keeps the conversation real.

statement.speaker: Keisha
statement.text: We bottled it in the second half, we had it wrapped up.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her team collapsed under pressure when they should have won
Her team played conservatively
Her team lost their nerve in the final minutes
Her team didn't try hard enough

payload.translation: Her team was winning comfortably but lost focus, made mistakes and the opponent came back. They had the game in their hands and let it slip away.

followUps.line: What changed in the second half?
Was it a defensive lapse or losing the ball?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Bottling happens to every team; don't minimise it but ask what went wrong.

statement.speaker: Amara
statement.text: They were clinical, one chance, one goal. We wasted ours.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The opponent took their few chances efficiently while her team missed theirs
The opponent had a doctor on the sideline
Her team created more chances but wasn't efficient
The opponent got lucky

payload.translation: The opponent finished their limited opportunities whereas her team created more chances but couldn't capitalise. Clinical means taking chances with precision.

followUps.line: Did your striker have a bad game?
How many shots did each team have?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Clinical finishing is a skill; it's fair to ask if the striker is normally sharp.

statement.speaker: Dev
statement.text: He nutmegged the full-back and cut it back for the tap-in.

payload.question: What does 'nutmeg' mean here?

options.text: Passing the ball between an opponent's legs
A skill move involving a spin
A sharp, quick dribble
A tap-in from a cutback

payload.translation: The winger flicked the ball through the full-back's legs (between their feet), beat him and then played a cutback pass for an easy finish.

followUps.why: Shows you understand the reward-risk trade.
Asks a real question about the player.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Skill moves are flashy; acknowledge the audacity without overdoing it.

payload.prompt: Match the fan slang to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A win that was messy, not dominant, but still earned the points.
A spectacular goal, often from distance.
Lost your nerve and threw away a winning position.
Taking your chances efficiently in front of goal.

explanation.summary: Four bits of fan slang cover a lot of match talk: the messy win, the wonder goal, the collapse and the ruthless finish.
explanation.sayThisLine: It was ugly, but we take the three points.

payload.template: Missing chances you should score is being {{a}}, while taking them coolly is being {{b}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Wasteful means missing the chances you should take, and clinical means finishing them efficiently.
explanation.incorrect: Wasteful is missing chances you should score, and clinical is finishing efficiently.
explanation.sayThisLine: We were wasteful today, they were clinical.

lessons.title: Season recap
lessons.objective: You can explain the season's big stories.

payload.prompt: In the Premier League, two teams finish level on points. What separates them first?

options.text: Goal difference
Head-to-head results
Alphabetical order

explanation.correct: Right. The Premier League ranks level teams by goal difference first. Some leagues, such as La Liga, look at head-to-head results first.
explanation.incorrect: Goal difference is the first tiebreaker in the Premier League. Rules differ by league, so always check which one you are talking about.

payload.template: In the Premier League, the {{bottom}} teams go down each season; the {{scrap}} is the fight for {{survival}}.

explanation.correct: Right. In the Premier League the three lowest teams are relegated, and the fight to escape them is the relegation scrap.
explanation.incorrect: The three teams at the bottom are relegated; the fight to escape that zone is called the relegation battle or scrap.

payload.prompt: The 2026 World Cup had 48 teams and was won by Spain, who beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time. True or false?

scene.alt: The 2026 World Cup final score: Spain 1 Argentina 0 (AET), with Spain celebrating.

explanation.correct: True. Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute in the 2026 final.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, Spain's Ferran Torres scored in extra time to win the 48-team 2026 World Cup.

statement.speaker: Ines
statement.text: It's a three-horse race and we've got the best run-in of all of them.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Three teams are fighting for the title
Her team has an easier fixture list at the end
Her team will definitely win
The other two teams are weaker

payload.translation: Three teams are level or close on points at the top. Her team has the advantage of facing easier opponents in their final matches, which could be crucial.

followUps.line: Do you think you'll hold on?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The run-in (fixture list) can decide a title. Ask who they're playing and gauge difficulty.

payload.prompt: Match the season-end battle to its stakes.

pairs.definition: The fight between the top teams for the league championship, decided by points and goal difference.
Teams battle for the top places that lead into the Champions League and other European competitions.
Teams near the bottom fight to avoid being relegated; every point is survival.

explanation.summary: The season has three overlapping dramas: who wins, who goes to Europe, and who gets relegated.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's tight at the top and tight at the bottom, the whole season's up for grabs.

statement.speaker: Carlos
statement.text: Ferran Torres in the 106th minute. I still get chills thinking about it.

payload.question: What is he talking about?

options.text: The 2026 World Cup final goal
A personal memory tied to a Spain goal
The winning goal of a major tournament
A recent club goal

payload.translation: Torres' goal in the 106th minute won the 2026 World Cup final for Spain (against Argentina). It's a big memory for fans.

followUps.line: Are you Spanish or just a Torres fan?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The 2026 final is recent history; sharing where you watched it connects you both.
